# After seven years of leaks, the ISS's PrK tunnel is reportedly shut for good

Russian cargo ships can no longer unload through it and will have to dock twice, Russianspaceweb reports. NASA and Roscosmos have not confirmed it.

By Orbinauts Published November 2, 2026, 2:57 PM UTC Updated November 2, 2026, 9:00 PM UTC 5 min read

Photograph: NASA (Public domain)

The partners in the International Space Station have decided to leave the PrK, the small transfer tunnel at the back of the Russian Zvezda module, permanently closed because of an air leak that cannot be stopped, Russianspaceweb reported on its 2026 page, last updated on 31 October. The site is the work of Anatoly Zak, a Moscow-born journalist who has covered the Russian space programme since the early 1990s, when he reported for the Moscow daily Nezavisimaya Gazeta. The public part of its page names no source, and neither NASA nor Roscosmos has announced the decision. But it matches what two NASA officials, speaking on background, told Ars Technica’s senior space editor, Eric Berger, in June: that Russia would decommission the tunnel.

...

The PrK is the short passage between Zvezda and the docking port at the station’s rear. That port receives Progress ships, Roscosmos’s uncrewed cargo ships, which each bring about three tons of food, fuel and supplies and leave months later full of rubbish to burn up in the atmosphere. To reach one and unload it, cosmonauts had to fill the tunnel with air, and its cracks leak each time the pressure goes up or down. A Progress at that port has a second job: it fires its engines to raise the station’s orbit, as Progress 91 is doing in the picture above.

## Two ports for every cargo ship

According to Russianspaceweb, the first ship to work the new way will be Progress MS-36 (Progress 97 in NASA’s numbering), which a Soyuz rocket is to launch from Baikonur on 24 November for a docking at the Poisk module on the 26th. Its cargo will be unloaded through Poisk’s open hatches. The ship will then move to the aft port, the best place to fire its engines because there they line up with the station’s main axis, though that port no longer gives a way into its cargo section. From then on this will be the rule: essentially every Progress will dock twice, once to unload and once to raise the station, until the station is deorbited as planned.

...

As the NASA officials described it, cosmonauts would no longer enter the PrK or try to pressurise it; Progress ships could still use its port to transfer fluids or for other work, and Russia would need other ports to bring supplies aboard. For NASA, that should retire the risk of a rapid depressurisation it had reluctantly accepted for years.

...

## Where the ships are now

In mid-October both ports MS-36 is to use were taken: NASA counted Progress 95 and 96 at the station. Progress 95 (MS-34 in Russia’s numbering) docked to Zvezda’s aft port on 27 April to stay about six months, a stay that ran out at the end of October; NASA has not reported it leaving. Progress 96 (MS-35) docked to Poisk on 19 September to stay about five months. Russianspaceweb lists Progress MS-37 for launch on 2 December, a week after MS-36. Neither NASA nor Russianspaceweb has said how the ships will be moved before 26 November.

## Who keeps the station up

Whichever ports the ships end up on, the station has to be raised again and again. Progress ships are not the only ones that do it: Northrop Grumman’s Cygnus XL raised it on 27 August, firing its thrusters for 20 minutes 43 seconds, and again on 25 September, for 18 minutes. According to Orbinauts, the average altitude of the ISS has dropped about 1.4 km in the five weeks since its last raise at the end of September, and on 2 November the station orbits between 415 and 425 km above the Earth.

# NASA, Northrop Grumman Complete Cygnus XL Space Station Reboost

Northrop Grumman’s Cygnus XL cargo craft is pictured installed to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port as the International Space Station orbited 262 miles above the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of South Africa.

Northrop Grumman’s Cygnus XL spacecraft today fired its thrusters for 20 mins, 43 seconds boosting the International Space Station’s orbit. 

The Cygnus XL’s gimbaled delta velocity engine was used to adjust the space station’s altitude by 2/10-of-a-mile at apogee, or highest point of station’s orbit, and 2.6 miles at perigee, or lowest point of station’s orbit, placing the station in an orbit of 266.5 x 254.9 miles. 

The Cygnus XL spacecraft, which is supporting NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 24 mission, arrived at the orbital complex on April 13, delivering more than 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the space station. Cygnus will remain berthed to space station until October when it will be filled with disposal cargo, unberthed from station, and then harmlessly burn up during its destructive reentry into Earth’s atmosphere.

This reboost sets up the phasing for Progress 96 launch in early September.

# Why Does the ISS Need to Be Reboosted?

 Tuesday, 20 October 2026 · 11 min read · By Orbital Radar Newsroom 

Image: NASA/JSC

Quick answer · as of 20 Oct 2026

Thin air still slows the ISS near 400 km above Earth. Periodic engine burns replace lost orbital energy and keep the station at a useful operating altitude.

Key figures · as of 20 Oct 2026 · Orbital Radar tracking data

| Active satellites | 15,874 |
| --- | --- |
| Starlink active | 10,081 |
| Catalogued objects | 31,835 |
| Predicted re-entries | 17 |
| Active close approaches | 22 |
| People in space | 10 |

The International Space Station (ISS) needs to be reboosted because atmospheric drag gradually removes orbital energy and lowers its orbit. Periodic engine burns replace that energy, keeping the station near its intended operating altitude.

The apparent paradox is that space near 400 km is an extremely good vacuum, but not an entirely empty one. Sparse gas still resists the station’s motion, causing orbital decay (the gradual lowering of an orbit).

...

The ISS has no fixed daily altitude loss: atmospheric density, station orientation and operational activity all affect how quickly its orbit decays. A daily-loss figure describes conditions over a particular interval, not a permanent property of the station. Changing the area presented to the thin atmosphere can change drag, even without a substantial change in altitude.

...

A reboost raises the ISS’s orbit by firing engines to add orbital energy, usually with thrust directed broadly along the station’s direction of travel. The burn initially increases its speed, changing the path it follows around Earth rather than lifting the entire orbital path at once.

The ISS is not being held up against gravity: it remains in continuous free ... The same principle applies across the satellite population.

...

## Which spacecraft can reboost the ISS?

Progress Spacecraft docks with the ISS during Expedition 12 · Image: NASA/JSC

Russian Progress cargo spacecraft have long provided propulsion for ISS reboosts, alongside engines on the Russian segment’s Zvezda service module. Northrop Grumman’s Cygnus cargo spacecraft has also performed reboosts, and SpaceX’s Dragon has demonstrated the capability.

That does not mean every visiting spacecraft, or every mission using those vehicles, routinely raises the station’s orbit. A demonstrated capability must be supported by the appropriate vehicle configuration, available propellant and an approved operational plan. Cargo delivery and reboost propulsion are distinct tasks, even when the same spacecraft performs both.

During a reboost by a visiting spacecraft, its engines push against the vehicle’s structure, and that force passes through the docking connection into the station. The ISS and its docked spacecraft therefore accelerate together. Engineers must select a suitable station orientation and keep forces within structural loading limits: the docking mechanism and station framework cannot simply accept an arbitrary push from any direction.

The docking location matters because it determines how the thrust acts on the combined structure. Planners also consider how much usable propellant remains, other demands on that fuel, crew activities and scheduled arrivals or departures. Orbital Radar’s station-keeping guide explains the wider role of these planned propulsion manoeuvres.

...

The ISS is reboosted according to an operational plan, not a universal fixed interval. Controllers schedule burns around the station’s changing orbit, visiting spacecraft and onboard activities, rather than simply repeating them after a set number of days.

Atmospheric drag gradually lowers the orbit. The timing and size of a reboost depend on how quickly altitude is being lost and the orbital altitude controllers want to maintain. A higher target generally reduces drag, but reaching it requires propellant and must remain compatible with other mission requirements.

Arriving spacecraft also influence that target. Their rendezvous plans depend on the station’s altitude and position along its orbit, so controllers can schedule a reboost to help establish suitable conditions for approach and docking.

The trade-offs include propellant use, crew schedules and research. Reboost acceleration briefly disturbs the near-weightless conditions that sensitive experiments require, so burns must be coordinated with station operations. Orbital Radar’s guide to station-keeping explains manoeuvres used to maintain an intended orbit.

...

Orbital Radar tracking data records 1,107 re-entries in 2026 as of 20 October. Orbital Radar tracking data also lists 17 predicted upcoming re-entries. Those catalogue-wide figures are not a countdown for the ISS.

Title: The Space Station Is Always Falling. Here's What Keeps It Up. — Daybreak Wire
URL: https://daybreakwire.com/science/iss-reboost-keeps-space-station-orbit/
Published: 2026-09-16T09:22:17.000Z
Author: Daniel Okafor
Highlights:
Roughly every few weeks to a few months, depending on solar activity and traffic scheduling, according to spaceflight blog Sentinel Mission. Recent burns show how routine, and how brief, the maneuver actually is. On Nov. 19, 2025, a docked Progress 93 cargo craft fired its engines from the aft port of the Zvezda service module for 14 minutes and 7 seconds, lifting the station's altitude by one mile at apogee and 2.3 miles at perigee. On April 16, 2026, the same spacecraft fired again for just over five minutes, this time to set up the station's orbital phase for the arrival of Progress 95.

Russian Progress spacecraft have handled most routine reboosts for decades because their docking port lines up almost exactly with the station's direction of travel, which wastes less thrust. But the job no longer belongs to Russia alone. SpaceX's Cargo Dragon demonstrated a boost-kit capability during its CRS-33 mission: a test burn on Sept. 3, 2025 raised the station about one mile at perigee, and a longer burn on Dec. 29, 2025, more than 19 minutes on two Draco engines, added 1.6 miles at apogee and 1.9 miles at perigee. Dragon performed six reboosts in total during that mission. Northrop Grumman's Cygnus spacecraft completed its own first limited reboost back on June 25, 2022, a five-minute-and-one-second burn that nudged the orbit by a tenth of a mile at apogee and half a mile at perigee.

Международную космическую станцию видно не каждый вечер: она появляется сезонами по одной-три недели, то после заката, то перед рассветом. Этот прогноз подскажет, когда её ждать в ноябре в вашем городе, в какие часы и какой вечер будет лучшим, чтобы не смотреть в небо наугад.

Коротко: в Москве, Казани, Екатеринбурге, Новосибирске и Минске в первой половине ноября станцию почти не видно (разве что один низкий пролёт перед рассветом 1 ноября), а примерно с 13–16 числа и до конца месяца начинается вечерний сезон: станцию видно в первые часы после заката, примерно с 17 до 21 часа по местному времени, в зависимости от города. ## Что происходит на станции в этом месяце

Ноябрь обещает быть насыщенным. Запланированы два выхода в открытый космос с американского сегмента: 29 октября и 5 ноября. It sounds like it should stay there forever, right? Wrong. Without regular intervention, atmospheric drag would pull the International Space Station (ISS) down into the atmosphere within just one or two years. To keep the station aloft, mission planners rely on a complex system of reboost providers-visiting cargo vehicles that fire their engines to lift the orbit back up. While Russian Progress ships have done the heavy lifting for decades, the landscape is shifting. Today, Northrop Grumman’s Cygnus and SpaceX’s Dragon are stepping into the role, creating a more resilient network for station operations.

For most of the ISS’s life, the primary reboost provider has been the Progress cargo spacecraft built by the Russian aerospace industry and operated by Roscosmos. These uncrewed vessels dock to the aft port of the Zvezda service module, which serves as the station’s main propulsion interface. Because Progress is specifically designed for this role, it handles the majority of routine altitude adjustments.

| Progress | Zvezda (Aft) | Primary / Routine | 1.0 - 1.67 m/s |
| Cygnus | Nadir (US Segment) | Certified Backup | ~0.9 m/s |
| Dragon | Nadir (US Segment) | Emerging / Tested | Variable |

Relying on a single nation for critical station maintenance carries geopolitical and technical risks. To mitigate this, NASA and its partners have worked to certify other vehicles for reboost duties. Enter Cygnus a cargo spacecraft developed by Northrop Grumman for resupply missions to the ISS. Unlike Progress, which docks to the Russian segment, Cygnus attaches to the US segment’s nadir port. This required significant engineering work to ensure the station could handle the thrust vectors correctly.

The certification process was cautious. The first attempt in June 2022 was aborted after just five seconds as a precaution. However, engineers refined the flight limits, and a subsequent burn on June 25, 2022, successfully raised the station’s altitude by roughly 0.8 km at perigee. By March 2023, Cygnus had completed a certified operational reboost, delivering 0.9 m/s of delta-V over 15 minutes. This maneuver was part of a series designed to set up orbital conditions for a Progress arrival, proving that Cygnus can now serve as a reliable secondary provider. As of mid-2026, Cygnus is no longer experimental; it is an integral part of the station’s propulsion redundancy strategy.

SpaceX Dragon a reusable spacecraft developed by SpaceX for crew and cargo transport to the ISS represents the next step in diversifying reboost capabilities. Historically, Dragon did not perform reboosts because it lacks the specific docking geometry or engine integration found in Progress. However, recent developments indicate this is changing. Analyses from late 2025 suggest that Dragon has become the latest craft to perform an ISS reboost test. This move is strategic: with the ISS scheduled for retirement around 2030, ensuring that multiple US-based vehicles can maintain the orbit reduces dependence on Russian assets during the station’s final operational years.

The challenge with non-Russian vehicles is the docking interface. Progress connects directly to the Zvezda module’s aft port, giving it direct control over the station’s attitude control thrusters. US vehicles dock to the Harmony module on the underside of the station. Using them for reboosts requires careful coordination to avoid destabilizing the station’s orientation. Nevertheless, qualifying Dragon adds another layer of security to the station’s orbital health.
